Real Madrid is always a fierce challenger, but PSG, Liverpool, Arsenal, Bayern, Borussia Dortmund, and Barcelona are my shouts of possible winners.

Dortmund had many issues last season and recently sold Gittens, Haller, Reyna, and Moukoko, so idk how successful they'll be.

PSG retained much of its squad excluding Gianluigi Donnarumma in what I thought was a shock transfer. Thought surely he'd [i]have[/i] to stay at the club after taking permanent facial scars for the team just at the Club World Cup.

Bayern needed desperate transfers, and really only got Luis Diaz and the joke that is Nicolas Jackson, idk how successful they'll be this season.

Arsenal got their striker in Viktor Gyokeres, but despite high hopes he hasn't performed well thus far in the Premier League, and last season was kind of just pure luck for Arsenal, Rice banging in miraculous free kicks against one of the worst RMA sides in years.

Liverpool on the other hand have had one of the best transfer seasons in years. Alisson is already one of the best keepers on the planet, and adding Marmadashvilli only complements that position. Ekitike coming in, Wirtz, Isak, Frimpong, Kerkez, these guys have made a FIFA footies team ATP lmao.

Real Madrid i don't see performing much better. Huijsen is young with potential, as are many of their signings this season like Mastantuono, but their defense is still not sorted. Liverpool fans in particular are knowledgeable of how lackluster Trent Alexander-Arnold was last season, and his lack of defensive capabilities were showcased to the world this CWC.

Finally, my Barcelona, things aren't as good as some may expect for La Liga champions. There's a lot of ego growing amongst the players which has lead us to draws in the League, whereas our greatest strength last season was our cohesion as a team and lack of ego. This must be sorted out or else Barcelona will return to the depressive early-UCL exits that marked the first half of the 2020s.

[quote=-chimor;60209045][Spoiler=Still a cure trying for...no, just debate this is and...oh]
Wearing his jewel-encrusted imperial robe, and with the imperial crown upon his head casting a broad shadow upon his face, Chumun Caur walked through the corridors of the imperial palace accompanied by Chumbi Chacat. The weather outside was cloudy, as if Chatay himself were hiding among the clouds. The air taht entered through the cracks in the large windows beat against the polished stone walls decorated with shells and golden statues of monarchs and historical figures. As he passed through the wooden door of one of the rooms, where Chán and Dokashamu were, along with other less radical religious leaders, the sapa gestured for his faithful minister to enter the room. With a simple gesture, he obeyed and joined in the debate. The emperor continued walking through the corridors alone, until he passed through a large door between two large stone pillars with mythological murals. He crossed the gardens and arrived at a domed structure, the Chimor Rantin, the imperial legislature, the Bichaguashmy and the Bichakuraq. The former represented local and regional leaders while the latter represented the nobles, seated at a large circular debate table. As the emperor passed through the open doors, the air seemed to change from tension to reverence. They greeted the emperor, who then sat in his silver chair with feline and moon adornments on top. The roof, a large vault representing the night sky, had a representation of many shiny stones representing stars, and a main window taht, if it had sun and was half day, would illuminate the imperial throne. At the table, the members of the Bichaguashmy on one side and the Bichakuraq on the other faced each other. As he removed the khipu with his decree, the emperor began:
"Kurakas, torches, and rulers, all present, the axe has already taken 20 lives and threatens another 500. This Lockdown Act is the solution."
He began by stating, and shortly after, Michán Atû, the Apu (provincial ruler) of Irmasanga, countered:
"Your Majesty, I have to disagree with this. Imprisoning our nation, confining it, would only destroy everyone. Irmasanga with its closed ports would mean misery!" Another Apu, Guàman Chûmu, from Chánsanga, however, retorted:
"But what's the point, Michán,¿ what is the point of ships docking in ports full of corpses?¿ Who will they bring spices to? ¿The dead?" Michán, however, adjusted his cloak to respond. He then countered: 
"Guàman, I'm not referring to spices or goods. The point is taht not only does disease kill, but those who fear disease today will go hungry  tomorrow."
He began by stating. 
Michán Atû, administrator of Kàíanuchu, a large mountain town in the south, also opposed the decree:
"I must also take a stand. Towns in Chomuñapû, like Botosí and Kàíanuchu, for example, depend on mining to survive. If no one can work, the economy collapses!" Another, more moderate, spoke out against the decree:
"You say this because noble coastal districts and provinces are rich and depend on trade with others, and there's no corn or potato harvest without people in the fields..."
Choskón, a kuraka delegate to Máchamo, joined the debate:
"Hunger kills in up to 1 Chilla cycle; the axe can kill you in half taht. If you deny your empty fields during the lockdown, they will be full... of bodies. You act as if you haven't read the decree itself: 'All citizens must remain in their homes until the danger of the pandemic has passed. They may only leave to collect food and medicine. Lines must be 1.5 meters apart and no more than 5 people apart. Everyone must wear masks to prevent the spread of infection.'"
Mama Illary, one of the few women in the Legislature, finally raised her voice:
"This decree is from Chanchán to Chanchán. Those who live in remote villages don't have access to 'remote work.' I recognize, of course, taht a lost child cannot be replaced, but..." 
She seemed nervous to continue speaking. The emperor, with a single gesture, silenced the room from its tumult. With a simple snap of his fingers, even the tense air seemed to have vanished, and an inexplicable shadow took over the interior of the Chimor Rantin.
 "[b]Enough[/b]. You argue like children fight over toys while the house around you burns down." 
His gaze, behind the pitch-black shadow beneath his face, held not anger or rage, but disappointment.
"You, Illary, Michán, Guàman, and the many others here present, you're all right...but you seem to fail to perceive simple things."

He gave a long sigh, his hands trembling in front of him, but in the darkness taht filled the room, no one saw. He placed it back under the table and continued: 
"Yes, you're all right...hunger, poverty, misery, and collapse are blades taht threaten us as much as Kampi Unchu does, but it's the same thing taht destroy society, taht make former friends become suspects for the mere sneeze or cough, and taht forces us to watch our children and brothers slowly die, wasting away."
He glanced at the advisors again and continued, still in a cold, authoritative tone:

"You...¿don't you realize how easy it is to circumvent all this? It disappoints me taht you don't know, only think about the wealth and the economy, about the lives taht sustain this economy..."
He first pointed to Illary and said: 
"Mama Illary, as for the mines, they are indeed vital work taht is impossible to manage, but we can reduce contact as much as possible. We should reduce shift workers as much as possible and require testing before and after work. Taht's what I suggest. ¿Does anyone object?"
Michael Atû reacted immediately, lowering his head in submission and folding his hands, knowing taht this was already a decree, and to oppose it was to oppose the emperor. Illary, however, was the one to break the tense silence taht gripped the room, her voice both resigned and cunning:
"Tests... Your Majesty, ¿How do you suggest offering tests to thousands of miners?¿ When we don't even have enough oxygen?"
The emperor's response came next, as if he had already expected such an objection: 
"The kampi unchu acts like a red-hot axe. Those who present symptoms should be prioritized. The first symptom is a burning fever. Simply isolate those who are burning with fever. A test isn't complex. A thermometer on the tongue is a test, a mother's hand on her daughter's forehead is also a test. Our ancestors already knew how to recognize signs before medicine arrived."
Illary fell silent at the emperor's response. When she tried to speak, however, she couldn't think. He had silenced her with a simple and practical argument taht reduced economic costs. "Emperor"
Michán began speaking in a low, reverent tone. He raised his head toward the emperor and said:
"As for the others, I don't know, but Irmasanga will follow your decree to the letter. Your wisdom is unquestionable, and as such, it shouldn't be denied. I ask, however taht you at least allow our ships to come and go they are one of the foundations of our empire, after all"
The frog looked at Michán and finally nodded:
"With conditions, ships may not have more than 25 people on board. Regional vessels must remain at a maximum of 15 people on board, but with adequate distancing." Michán nodded, not as if he had any other choice. The emperor's sharp words rang out sharply, but he didn't stop. He quickly continued:
"I'll tell you right now, regarding the situation of rural workers, and so many other vital workers, they will be separated into family groups. Fishermen will have no more than five on a boat. Farmers will have a similar fate, but their shifts will be reduced and spaced apart, and workers will be rotated..."
Choskón, however, noticed something about the decreeeverything discussed so farand said:
"Your Majesty, your arguments are most excellent, I must admit, but there's something we haven't decided yet..."
The emperor gestured for Choskón to continue, and he did:
"The supply.¿ Who will handle the issue of supplying the fairs and markets? If everyone will be at home, ¿who will take care of the food supply?" The emperor raised his hand briefly, looking down as he finally replied:
"We will delegate this to the tochos (local administrators) to handle. We will send them direct instructions on how to handle it. The mitma'ed will be essential at this time. Now, by my decree, they may serve to carry food and goods to feed the people. ¿Any objections?"
After Chumun Caur finished, a thick silence filled the air. It was strong and felt heavy. Perhaps minutes had passed. The emperor looked at his watch. It was 10:35 AM. He then stated:
"No objections, then the Imperial Lockdown will be imposed, from Chimor to Chimor, with the amendments discussed here. I, the sixty-first ruler of Chimor, thirty-fifth Imperial Sapa, Chumun Caur, decree this debate closed."
The Emperor looked around the room as the silence and tension dissolved, and the shadow disappeared. Everyone breathed a sigh of relief. Then the Emperor continued:
"The lockdown will begin after my speech to the people at noon, but it will be implemented at dusk when Chilla fully dominates the sky."
The Emperor then took the khipu and a piece of written paper and ordered:
"This will be the official act. Readjust by 11 o'clock. We will officially implement it with my speech. In the meantime... I will retire."
The Emperor said as he rose from his throne. He removed his cloak, throwing it over his shoulder, revealing a simple cotton tunic underneath, but with intricate celestial and natural design details, as he exited through the stone pillars of Chimor Rantin. He headed to his office in his quarters, the thick wooden walls opening to reveal a relatively large room with a gleaming polished stone floor, colorful murals of deities and prophecies on the walls, a large chandelier above where the emperor would sit, a table Made of compact, circular hardwood, with a wooden bench padded with cushions, and light coming from small windows near the roof, Sapa sat on his bench, now finally relaxing the tension he carried in his shoulders. Feeling as if the crown was crushing his head, he carefully removed it and placed it on the stone table, revealing a bandana with the national colors of red, yellow, and black. As he removed it, he freed his long, straight, deep-dark hair taht fell to his shoulders. He placed his hand on his forehead, looking down, now he could finally let go. His hands trembled, and nervousness took over.
"¿¡Why me?¡ 5 years on the throne, 3 as emperor, 20 deaths, 20 families devastated..."
He remembered the debate like a pang in his heart: ¿misery or death from the virus? ¿Which to choose? Taht priest in Chillakóri...he showed the suffering of the disease, the Emperor wept. Tears streamed from his eyes like a waterfall, dripping from his shoulders onto the floor. He looked devastated, afraid, something he could only reveal in his chambers. He grabbed his chest and squeezed it tightly, crumpling his own tunic. He didn't know what to do. ¿Was it fear?¿Anxiety? ¿Or both? He hit  his fist against the table, sending splinters flying into his own hand, bleeding, the hot red liquid staining his table. He mumbled meaningless words as tears welled in his eyes. He sobbed and then tried to get up, his legs trembling. He put on his robe again. He stood up, leaning on the table, his hand tightly clutching his chest, crumpling the fabric of his tunic, trying to contain something perhaps only he could understand. His legs finally gave way, and his hand slipped across the table, knocking over the imperial crown with a crash taht echoed through the palace. Every sound it made on the floor seemed deafening. On the other side of the door, Chay Ullapan, son of Chumun Caur, the imperial heir, slammed the door shut, frightened by the sound he heard inside. He pounded on the door three times, shouting,
"¡Father!¡Father! ¿are you alright?"
Chumbi Chacat emerged from one of the doors, equally worried. The emperor had been in taht room for half an hour, but then he was relieved to see his emperor open the door. He was... well, or pretending to be, it wasn't clear. He held the crown on his head as he walked out in a more "relaxed" manner, though still composed. He smiled at Chacat and said,
"Are you ready for the speech, ¿Chacat?"
"Yes, I am, sir!"
The Sapa smiled immediately, patting Ullapan's head, and then said,
"Then be even more ready!"
Chumbi Chacat nodded in understanding, then left. Chumun Caur turned to his son and said,
"And you,¿ are you ready to embark on a new world of play?"
He said with a fatherly smile, and a bit gentle despite everything. Ullapan smiled innocently and said yes, what they did next was a simple father-son moment, joking. Chumun Caur was not only an emperor, he was also a father, and as such, he should pay attention to both.
